title: What a Throw Does on the Way Out: Catching by Reference, Rethrowing, and the Destructors That Run

questions.question: A function throws std::invalid_argument("bad value 12abc") and the caller writes catch (std::exception e). What does the handler hold?
options: A std::exception copied from the base part
questions.explanation: It is no longer an invalid_argument, and on some libraries the message is gone too. Caught by reference it kept both the type and the message.

questions.question: What is the right way to write a handler for a specific exception?
options: By const reference, most specific handler first

questions.question: What is the difference between throw e; and throw; inside a handler?
options: throw e; throws a copy made from the declared type of e, throw
questions.explanation: Rethrows the very object with its own type. throw e; gave cut down to exception, throw; gave still invalid_argument.

questions.question: What does parse_all do before rethrowing?
options: It records which item failed, then uses a bare throw
questions.explanation: So the caller still sees the original type. The caller learns both where and what.

questions.question: Three guards A, B, C are alive when a throw happens. In what order do things happen?
options: drop A, B, C, then the handler
handler, then drop A, B, C
drop C, drop B, drop A, then the handler
questions.explanation: Reverse order of construction, before the handler starts. That is why cleanup belongs in a destructor.

questions.question: A function releases a motor on the line after a call that can throw. What happens when it throws?
questions.explanation: A throw leaves at once and only destructors run on the way out. Put the release in a destructor so the unwinding does it.
